Seventy healthy young adults were recruited through convenience sampling from the Faculty of Psychology and Speech Therapy at the Universitat de València, Spain.

Two participants were excluded from analyses due to incomplete data resulting from technical errors during administration of the computerized task, yielding a final sample of 68 (58 women, 10 men; M age = 18.94 years, SD = 1.46, range: 18-23), which remained within the a priori target range and provided approximately 74-80% power across the anticipated effect size range.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Sample size was determined a priori using G*Power 3.1. Based on effect sizes reported in prior studies examining the relationship between anxiety and decisionmaking parameters under risk (e.g., Pabst et al., 2013), a small-to-medium effect size was anticipated (f² = 0.15-0.20) for the primary moderation analyses (linear multiple regression, k = 3 predictors, α = .05). This range corresponded to target sample sizes of 60-77 participants to achieve 80% statistical power. A target of 70 participants was therefore established.

Seventy healthy young adults were recruited through convenience sampling from the Faculty of Psychology and Speech Therapy at the Universitat de València, Spain. Two participants were excluded from analyses due to incomplete data resulting from technical errors during administration of the computerized task, yielding a final sample of 68 (58 women, 10 men; M age = 18.94 years, SD = 1.46, range: 18-23), which remained within the a priori target range and provided approximately 74-80% power across the anticipated effect size range. The sample was predominantly of Spanish origin (85.51%), with a medium-to-high socioeconomic level (M = 3.10, SD = 0.52). Exclusion criteria included any current neurological or psychiatric diagnosis, habitual drug use, and substance consumption (alcohol or other drugs) within the 24 hours prior to the experimental session. All participants provided written informed consent. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Universitat de València (Reference: 2023-PSILOG-2558999), in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

marginal.title: Marginal Significance
marginal.summary_text: You described 3 effects with terms related to 'marginally significant'.

table.text: Alexithymia moderated both effects through distinct conditional patterns: the self-reported hyperarousal-choice consistency association was significant only below a TAS-20 threshold of 51.05 (67.65% of the sample), reflecting monotonic buffering; the self-reported hyperarousal-value sensitivity association was significant within a bounded TAS-20 range (45.31-66.08), suggesting that intermediate alexithymia constitutes a zone of maximal vulnerability, though this model only reached trend significance and should be treated as exploratory.
However, the overall regression model only reached a trend of significance, F(3, 64) = 2.46, p= .071, R² = .103.

The present data provide preliminary behavioral decisionlevel support for this characterization; however, given that the overall regression model for value sensitivity only reached a trend of significance, these results should be interpreted with caution and treated as exploratory, pending replication with larger samples that afford adequate statistical power to detect moderation effects of this size.

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 2 imprecise *p* values out of 10 detected *p* values.

table.formatted: No significant gender differences were found for any variable (all ps > .05), and thus subsequent analyses were conducted on the full sample without gender stratification.
table.expanded: No significant gender differences were found for any variable (all ps > .05), and thus subsequent analyses were conducted on the full sample without gender stratification.
The overall model accounted for 11.2% of the variance in τ, F(3, 64) = 2.68, p= .05, R² = .112.
Hyperarousal was a significant main predictor (B = -0.0043, SE = 0.002, t = -1.99, p= .049), indicating that higher hyperarousal was associated with lower choice consistency.

Alexithymia was not significant as a main effect (p= .112), but the hyperarousal × alexithymia interaction achieved significance (B = 0.001, SE = 0.0001, t = 1.97, p= .05), suggesting that the effect of hyperarousal on choice consistency varies as a function of alexithymia levels.

Alexithymia was not significant as a main effect (p= .112), but the hyperarousal × alexithymia interaction achieved significance (B = 0.001, SE = 0.0001, t = 1.97, p= .05), suggesting that the effect of hyperarousal on choice consistency varies as a function of alexithymia levels.

Hyperarousal was also a significant individual predictor of value sensitivity (B = -0.007, SE = 0.0015, t = -2.44, p= .017), suggesting that higher hyperarousal is associated with reduced value sensitivity; that is, greater risk aversion through diminished sensitivity to outcome magnitudes.

table.formatted: The hyperarousal × alexithymia interaction was likewise significant (B = -0.0001, SE = 0.0001, t = -2.01, p= .04), and the Johnson-Neyman analysis identified a bounded region of significance for TAS-20 values between 45.31 (95% CI [-0.0019, 0.000]) and 66.08 (95% CI [-0.0022, 0.000]), within which hyperarousal significantly predicted reduced value sensitivity (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2B</ref>).
table.expanded: The hyperarousal × alexithymia interaction was likewise significant (B = -0.0001, SE = 0.0001, t = -2.01, p= .04), and the Johnson-Neyman analysis identified a bounded region of significance for TAS-20 values between 45.31 (95% CI [-0.0019, 0.000]) and 66.08 (95% CI [-0.0022, 0.000]), within which hyperarousal significantly predicted reduced value sensitivity (see Figure 2B).
However, the overall regression model only reached a trend of significance, F(3, 64) = 2.46, p= .071, R² = .103.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. table.text: Hyperarousal was a significant main predictor (B = -0.0043, SE = 0.002, t = -1.99, p= .049), indicating that higher hyperarousal was associated with lower choice consistency.

Alexithymia was not significant as a main effect (p= .112), but the hyperarousal × alexithymia interaction achieved significance (B = 0.001, SE = 0.0001, t = 1.97, p= .05), suggesting that the effect of hyperarousal on choice consistency varies as a function of alexithymia levels.

Hyperarousal was also a significant individual predictor of value sensitivity (B = -0.007, SE = 0.0015, t = -2.44, p= .017), suggesting that higher hyperarousal is associated with reduced value sensitivity; that is, greater risk aversion through diminished sensitivity to outcome magnitudes.

The hyperarousal × alexithymia interaction was likewise significant (B = -0.0001, SE = 0.0001, t = -2.01, p= .04), and the Johnson-Neyman analysis identified a bounded region of significance for TAS-20 values between 45.31 (95% CI [-0.0019, 0.000]) and 66.08 (95% CI [-0.0022, 0.000]), within which hyperarousal significantly predicted reduced value sensitivity (see Figure 2B).
However, the overall regression model only reached a trend of significance, F(3, 64) = 2.46, p= .071, R² = .103.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Universitat de València (Reference: 2023-PSILOG-2558999), in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
live_data_statements: Seventy healthy young adults were recruited through convenience sampling from the Faculty of Psychology and Speech Therapy at the Universitat de València, Spain.

Two participants were excluded from analyses due to incomplete data resulting from technical errors during administration of the computerized task, yielding a final sample of 68 (58 women, 10 men; M age = 18.94 years, SD = 1.46, range: 18-23), which remained within the a priori target range and provided approximately 74-80% power across the anticipated effect size range.
All participants provided written informed consent.
In each of 64 trials, participants were presented with a gamble offering a potential gain and a potential loss and decided whether to accept or reject it (see Figure 1).
